full_title: PETRONILO SOLOMON SARIGUMBA, PETITIONER, VS. COMMISSION ON ELECTIONS, REPRESENTED BY CAMPAIGN FINANCE UNIT, RESPONDENT.
subject: Political and Public International Law
syllabus_topic: VIII. Constitutional Rights > N. Rights to Speedy Trial and Speedy Disposition of Cases
topics: Inordinate delay in the COMELEC's preliminary investigation of an election offense
Cagang framework: burden shifts to the prosecution when prescribed periods are exceeded
Failure to file a counter-affidavit does not suspend the period to resolve (COMELEC Rules, Rule 34, Secs. 6 and 8)
Election overspending (OEC Sec. 100 in relation to Sec. 262, as amended by RA 7166)
Exceptions to the prior motion for reconsideration before certiorari

doctrine:
The right to a speedy disposition of cases under **Article III, Section 16 of the Constitution** may be invoked in a preliminary investigation conducted by the COMELEC. Applying *Cagang v. Sandiganbayan*, once the delay goes beyond the prescribed periods, **the burden shifts to the prosecution** to prove that it followed the prescribed procedure, that the complexity of the issues and the volume of evidence made the delay inevitable, and that the respondent suffered no prejudice.

**A respondent's failure to file a counter-affidavit does not give the COMELEC license to delay the preliminary investigation indefinitely.** Rule 34, Sections 6 and 8 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure must be read together: if the respondent does not file a counter-affidavit within the 10-day period, the investigating officer must resolve the complaint on the complainant's evidence, and **the 20-day period to conclude the preliminary investigation (plus five days to resolve) is counted from the lapse of the period to file the counter-affidavit**. A delay of over six years in resolving a simple overspending complaint against one respondent, decided only on his own Statement of Election Contributions and Expenditures (SOCE), is inordinate. The Court applied *Peñas v. COMELEC* and *Peralta v. COMELEC* even though the respondents there filed counter-affidavits and the petitioner here did not.

Reiterating *Peñas* and *Cervantes v. Sandiganbayan*, a respondent is not duty-bound to follow up his case, and he may invoke the right after the adverse resolution, unless the delay is directly attributable to him. Because inordinate delay alone merits dismissal, a prior motion for reconsideration may be dispensed with. The remedy is the **nullification of the resolution finding probable cause and the dismissal of the complaint**.
facts:
Petitioner Petronilo Solomon Sarigumba ran for mayor of Loboc, Bohol in the May 10, 2010 elections and lost. On June 10, 2010, he filed his SOCE, which reported contributions and expenditures of PHP 143,000.00. On November 3, 2014, he received a letter dated October 1, 2014 from the head of the COMELEC Campaign Finance Unit (CFU) requiring him to explain his alleged overspending. He submitted an Explanation dated November 27, 2014.

Based on the COMELEC's own timeline, the CFU filed a *motu proprio* Complaint on December 20, 2014 for overspending under Section 100 in relation to Section 262 of the Omnibus Election Code (OEC), as amended by RA 7166. The preliminary investigation was set on April 14, 2015, but only the complainant's representative appeared. Petitioner's counsel sought a resetting to May 12, 2015 because petitioner was unfit to travel, which was granted. On May 12, 2015, counsel filed an omnibus motion to cancel the setting and to delegate the investigation to the provincial COMELEC officer. An Order dated June 11, 2015 denied the motion and directed petitioner to subscribe his counter-affidavit before a public prosecutor and send it by registered mail or courier. Petitioner never filed one.

On July 27, 2021, the COMELEC Law Department found probable cause. It reasoned that as a party member, petitioner could spend only PHP 3.00 per voter, or PHP 30,816.00 for Loboc's 10,272 registered voters, yet his SOCE showed PHP 143,000.00 in expenses. On July 28, 2021, the COMELEC En Banc adopted the recommendation in Minute Resolution No. 21-0499-24, which petitioner received on August 18, 2022.

Without moving for reconsideration, petitioner filed a Rule 64 petition for certiorari in relation to Rule 65, claiming inordinate delay and invoking *Peñas*. He also asked for a writ of preliminary injunction. The COMELEC, through the OSG, argued that petitioner failed to file a motion for reconsideration; that the period to resolve never began to run because he filed no counter-affidavit; and that he waived the right by not invoking it on time and by not taking part in the preliminary investigation.
issues: Whether the petition for certiorari may be entertained even though petitioner did not first move for reconsideration of the COMELEC En Banc Minute Resolution.
Whether the COMELEC violated petitioner's right to a speedy disposition of his case, so that the finding of probable cause must be nullified and the complaint dismissed.
ruling:
**1. Yes, a motion for reconsideration was not required.** As a rule, certiorari will not lie unless a motion for reconsideration is first filed. The exceptions include an urgent necessity for resolution where further delay would prejudice the petitioner, cases where a motion for reconsideration would be useless, and cases where public interest is involved. Because the proceedings were attended by inordinate delay, which "alone merits the dismissal of the *motu proprio* Complaint," a motion for reconsideration would have been futile.

**2. Yes, the right was violated.** Following *Cagang*, the right to speedy disposition may be invoked in the COMELEC's preliminary investigation. The proceedings ran from December 20, 2014 to July 28, 2021, or six years and over seven months, and six years and over one month from the June 11, 2015 Order directing petitioner to file a counter-affidavit. The COMELEC's argument that the period never ran because no counter-affidavit was filed relied on Rule 34, Section 8 alone. **Reading Section 8 with Section 6, failure to file a counter-affidavit does not give the COMELEC "unbridled license to indefinitely toll or delay" the investigation; the 20-day period runs from the lapse of the period to file the counter-affidavit.** The COMELEC never stated when petitioner received the June 11, 2015 Order or when his deadline lapsed, and the Court took that silence against it. Given the length of the delay, the COMELEC plainly failed to observe the 20-day and five-day periods, so it bore the burden of justifying the delay.

It did not discharge that burden. The case involved no complex issues or voluminous records: the Law Department relied only on petitioner's SOCE and a simple computation of the spending limit. As in *Peñas* and *Peralta*, which involved the same kind of *motu proprio* overspending complaints against 2010 mayoral candidates that took the COMELEC about six years or more to resolve, the delay was unjustified. That the petitioners there filed counter-affidavits made no difference, because the COMELEC Rules required the investigating officer to resolve the case even without one. Petitioner's two motions in April and May 2015 did not cause substantial delay; from the lapse of the period to file the counter-affidavit, the delay was the COMELEC's. Nor could petitioner be faulted for invoking the right only after the adverse resolution: it is the duty of the prosecutor to resolve the complaint speedily "regardless of whether the petitioner did not object to the delay or that the delay was with his acquiescence provided that it was not due to causes directly attributable to him" (*Cervantes*, reiterated in *Peñas*). **The Minute Resolution was therefore tainted with grave abuse of discretion; it must be nullified and the complaint dismissed.**
disposition: Petition GRANTED. COMELEC En Banc Minute Resolution No. 21-0499-24 dated July 28, 2021 was NULLIFIED for having been rendered with grave abuse of discretion amounting to lack or excess of jurisdiction. The *motu proprio* Complaint against Petronilo Solomon Sarigumba for election overspending under Section 100 in relation to Section 262 of the OEC, as amended by RA 7166, was DISMISSED.

bar_questions.q: Lorenzo lost the 2019 mayoral elections and filed his Statement of Election Contributions and Expenditures. In January 2020, the COMELEC Law Department filed a motu proprio complaint against him for overspending, based solely on his SOCE. In March 2020, Lorenzo received a subpoena requiring him to file his counter-affidavit within 10 days, but he never filed one. In 2026, the COMELEC En Banc found probable cause and directed the filing of an Information. Lorenzo files a petition for certiorari invoking his right to a speedy disposition of cases. The COMELEC argues that (1) the period to resolve the complaint never began to run because Lorenzo never filed a counter-affidavit, and (2) Lorenzo waived the right because he never followed up on his case or objected to the delay. Rule on the COMELEC's arguments.

alac.answer: Both arguments fail. The COMELEC committed inordinate delay, and the finding of probable cause should be nullified and the complaint dismissed.
alac.legal_basis: Article III, Section 16 of the Constitution guarantees the speedy disposition of cases before all judicial, quasi-judicial and administrative bodies, including the COMELEC's preliminary investigation. Under Rule 34, Sections 6 and 8 of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure, read together, if the respondent does not file a counter-affidavit within 10 days, the investigating officer resolves the case on the complainant's evidence, and the 20-day period to conclude the investigation runs from the lapse of the period to file the counter-affidavit. Once the prescribed periods are exceeded, the prosecution must justify the delay (Cagang v. Sandiganbayan). A respondent is not duty-bound to follow up his case; the prosecutor must resolve it speedily even if the respondent did not object, unless the delay is directly attributable to him. (Sarigumba v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 263615, August 19, 2025)
alac.application: (1) Lorenzo's 10-day period lapsed in March 2020. From then, the COMELEC had to conclude the investigation within 20 days and resolve it within five days on the evidence it had. Taking about six years violates those periods, so the burden shifted to the COMELEC. The case was simple, involving one respondent and a computation based on his own SOCE, so complexity cannot justify the delay. (2) Lorenzo's silence is not a waiver: the duty to resolve the complaint rests on the COMELEC, and nothing shows that the delay was caused by Lorenzo.
alac.conclusion: The COMELEC violated Lorenzo's right to a speedy disposition of his case, so its resolution finding probable cause should be nullified and the complaint dismissed.

bar_questions.q: In a motu proprio overspending complaint filed by the COMELEC in 2021, respondent Dante moved to reset the preliminary investigation nine times over three years, citing his schedule and his counsel's other hearings, and filed two motions to transfer the investigation to another office. He finally filed his counter-affidavit in 2024. The COMELEC concluded the investigation and found probable cause within a month after receiving his counter-affidavit. Dante files certiorari, claiming that the three years from the filing of the complaint violated his right to a speedy disposition of cases, citing Sarigumba v. COMELEC. Will his petition prosper?

alac.answer: No. The delay is attributable to Dante, not to the COMELEC.
alac.legal_basis: Under Cagang v. Sandiganbayan, as applied in Sarigumba v. COMELEC (G.R. No. 263615, August 19, 2025), the length of delay is never computed mechanically; courts consider the entire context and the causes of the delay, which must be properly laid out, and delay caused by the respondent's own acts is not charged to the prosecution. The prosecutor's duty to resolve the complaint speedily holds regardless of the respondent's silence "provided that it was not due to causes directly attributable to him" (Cervantes v. Sandiganbayan, reiterated in Peñas and Sarigumba). In Sarigumba, the Court counted the delay against the COMELEC only from the lapse of the period to file the counter-affidavit, finding that the respondent's two early motions had not caused substantial delay.
alac.application: Unlike in Sarigumba, where the COMELEC let the case sit for six years after the counter-affidavit period lapsed, here the three-year delay came from Dante's own repeated requests for resetting and motions to transfer. Once he filed his counter-affidavit, the COMELEC resolved the case within a month, well within its prescribed periods. Dante cannot profit from a delay he caused.
alac.conclusion: Dante's petition will not prosper because the delay was directly attributable to him.

bar_questions.q: The COMELEC En Banc issued a minute resolution finding probable cause to charge Mayor Ana with an election offense, more than six years after the complaint was filed against her, with no explanation for the delay. Ana did not move for reconsideration. (a) What remedy should Ana file with the Supreme Court, and may she file it without first moving for reconsideration? (b) If her petition is granted, what relief will the Court give?

alac.answer: (a) A petition for certiorari under Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 of the Rules of Court, which she may file without a prior motion for reconsideration. (b) The Court will nullify the resolution finding probable cause and dismiss the complaint.
alac.legal_basis: As a rule, certiorari does not lie unless a motion for reconsideration is first filed, but the requirement is excused where there is an urgent necessity for resolution and further delay would prejudice the petitioner, where a motion for reconsideration would be useless, or where public interest is involved. Inordinate delay in the preliminary investigation is grave abuse of discretion, and the remedy is to nullify the resolution and dismiss the case. (Sarigumba v. COMELEC, G.R. No. 263615, August 19, 2025)
alac.application: (a) Ana is assailing a COMELEC En Banc resolution, so the remedy is Rule 64 in relation to Rule 65 on the ground of grave abuse of discretion. Because the proceedings were attended by unexplained delay of over six years, which by itself warrants dismissal, a motion for reconsideration would be futile, and the right to speedy disposition involves public interest and urgency. (b) If the Court finds inordinate delay, the resolution is tainted with grave abuse of discretion; the proper relief is to nullify it and dismiss the complaint, not merely to order the COMELEC to act faster.
alac.conclusion: Ana may go directly to the Supreme Court on certiorari under Rule 64, and if she proves inordinate delay, the resolution will be nullified and the complaint dismissed.

notes: The petition alleged that the CFU complaint was filed on February 10, 2015; the Court used December 20, 2014, the filing date in the COMELEC's own timeline. In summarizing the COMELEC's argument, the Decision refers to "Rule 3, Section 8" of the COMELEC Rules of Procedure, but the Court's analysis applies Rule 34, Sections 6 and 8. The Court did not separately rule on the prayer for a writ of preliminary injunction. Kho, Jr., J. took no part (a footnote lists him among the COMELEC Commissioners who signed the assailed Minute Resolution); Singh, J. was on leave.
